content: 1. Glucagon enhances the effects of atropine by increasing the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions due to additive inhibition of gastrointestinal motility. Co-administration of anticholinergic drugs and glucagon should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 2. Glucagon increases the toxicity of benztropine by similar mechanisms, leading to heightened gastrointestinal risks. Avoid co-administration or use alternative medications. 3. Glucagon reduces the toxicity of beta-blockers such as betaxolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol, celiprolol, esmolol, labetalol, metoprolol, nadolol, nebivolol, penbutolol, pindolol, propranolol, sotalol, and timolol by sympathetic adrenergic effects, including transient increases in blood pressure and heart rate. Use caution and monitor closely during co-administration. 4. Glucagon increases the toxicity of anticholinergic drugs such as dicyclomine, glycopyrrolate (oral and inhaled), hyoscyamine (oral and spray), ipratropium, methscopolamine, scopolamine, tiotropium, trihexyphenidyl, tropicamide, and umeclidinium bromide (alone or in combination with vilanterol). This is due to additive effects on gastrointestinal motility inhibition, increasing the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 5. Indomethacin decreases the effects of glucagon through an unknown mechanism, potentially reducing its ability to raise blood glucose levels or even causing hypoglycemia. Use caution and monitor closely. 6. Glucagon decreases the effects of various forms of insulin (e.g., insulin aspart, insulin aspart protamine/insulin aspart, insulin degludec, insulin degludec/insulin aspart, insulin detemir, insulin glargine, insulin glulisine, inhaled insulin, insulin isophane human/insulin regular human, insulin lispro, insulin lispro protamine/insulin lispro, insulin NPH, and insulin regular human) by pharmacodynamic antagonism. This occurs because glucagon, as a regulatory hormone, increases blood glucose levels. Exogenous glucagon is often used to treat hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes mellitus. Use caution and monitor closely. 7. Glucagon increases the effects of warfarin when doses exceed 50 mg over a 2-day period. Use caution and monitor closely. 8. Glucagon is contraindicated in patients with pheochromocytoma, as it may stimulate the release of catecholamines from the tumor, leading to a dramatic increase in blood pressure. If this occurs, 5-10 mg of phentolamine mesylate can be used to lower blood pressure temporarily. 9. When used as a diagnostic tool, glucagon may increase myocardial oxygen demand, blood pressure, and pulse rate, which can be life-threatening in patients with cardiac disease. Cardiac monitoring is recommended during use in such patients, and any increase in blood pressure or pulse rate may require therapy. 10. Generalized allergic reactions, including urticaria, respiratory distress, and hypotension, have been reported with glucagon use. If symptoms occur, discontinue use and treat as indicated. 11. Glucagon is effective in treating hypoglycemia only if sufficient hepatic glycogen is present. Patients in states of starvation, with adrenal insufficiency, or with chronic hypoglycemia may not have adequate hepatic glycogen levels for therapy to be effective. In such cases, glucose should be used instead.
